doc.title: Vince Giordano interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

title: Early jazz in the Navy band and reactions to it
summary: Few Navy bandmates cared for early jazz; he talks about negative comments and keeping early styles alive alongside modern ones.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: And so in the military band, are you looking for people who have a like mind hoping that you might get some converts?

Yeah. I only had one fellow that really wanted to play early jazz. He was a guitarist but he played a little cornet. And I was playing banjo in the band also, tuba, electric bass and banjo. And we would jam together and he got to use his cornet chops. But none of the other fellows really could see what I was doing at all. They would just kind of, you know, roll their eyes and raise their eyebrows to anyone that was interested in any kind of interest in this early archaic music. And I said, again, no problem.
“Archaic” is an interesting word. Part of it I think, do people have a hard time with the fidelity of it?
You know, that sort of ancient delivery system. Did it help at all when things started being reissued on CD or remastered?

Yeah that was pre-CD, that was still LPs and cassettes and all that stuff. You know I still get a lot of negative comments about what I’m doing. And I don’t have any problem with music or jazz going as far as you want it to go, but not to just abandon or throw out some of the early styles. I mean we still play Mozart, Brahms and Beethoven along with Philip Glass and who everyone else say is contemporary, I don’t know, I don’t keep up with everybody just for a name. And they all should survive. But not to say well we shouldn’t listen to these early classical masters, you know. And there’s some people who take me to task for that.
